Ontological is an adjective that means relating to the nature and fact of existence itself.

To understand it properly, you need to first understand its root noun: ontology. Ontology is the branch of philosophy that asks the most radical, foundational question a human mind can ask — not "how do things work?" or "how do we know things?" but simply:

"What exists? And what does it mean for something to exist at all?"

That's it. That's the whole game. Ontology sits at the very bottom of all human thinking, underneath science, underneath religion, underneath common sense — it's the bedrock question of reality itself.

So when you describe something as ontological, you're saying it has to do with the existence, being, or fundamental nature of something — not just its properties or behavior, but whether it is real, what kind of thing it is, and what its existence actually consists of.
Making It Click: The Three Layers of Questions

Imagine you're looking at a tree. You could ask three very different kinds of questions about it:

  • Practical question: "How tall is that tree? Is the wood strong enough to build with?"
  • Scientific question: "How does the tree photosynthesize? What species is it?"
  • Ontological question: "What does it mean for this tree to exist? Is it a single thing, or just a collection of cells? When it dies and decomposes, does it still exist in some form? Is the 'tree' a real thing in nature, or just a label we invented?"

The third type of question is ontological. It drills all the way down to existence itself, not just the tree's qualities or functions.
The Most Famous Example: The Ontological Argument

The most well-known use of this word in all of philosophy is the Ontological Argument for the existence of God, proposed by the medieval philosopher Anselm.

The argument goes roughly like this:

  1. God is defined as the greatest possible being that can be conceived.
  2. A being that actually exists in reality is greater than one that only exists as an idea in the mind.
  3. Therefore, God must exist in reality — because if God didn't, God wouldn't be the greatest possible being.

Notice what makes this argument ontological: it is entirely about existence and the nature of being. Anselm isn't pointing to the stars, to miracles, or to history. He is reasoning purely from the concept of what God is to whether God exists. That move — from the nature of a thing to its existence — is the signature move of ontological thinking.

Whether or not the argument is convincing is a separate debate (and it is deeply debated). The point is that it earns the label "ontological" because it operates purely in the realm of existence and being.
Common Ways the Word Is Used

Here are the main contexts where you will encounter "ontological," explained clearly:

1. Ontological status
This phrase asks: does something truly exist, and if so, what kind of existence does it have?

For example: "What is the ontological status of numbers?"
Numbers like 7 or π are not physical objects — you can't hold a 7 in your hand. But they feel very real, and mathematics works perfectly. So do numbers exist? If yes, in what sense? Are they things "out there" in the universe, or are they inventions of the human mind? That question is a question of ontological status.

2. Ontological commitment
When you make a statement, you are often quietly committing yourself to the existence of certain things. This is your ontological commitment.

For example, if you say "the average American has 2.3 children," you are committing yourself to the idea that "the average American" is in some sense a real thing you can describe — even though no actual human has 2.3 children. Philosophers ask: does saying this force you to believe such an entity really exists? That question is about ontological commitment.

3. Ontological categories
These are the most fundamental types or kinds of things that exist. For instance: objects, properties, events, relations, minds, numbers. Sorting all of reality into its most basic buckets is the work of building an ontological framework.

4. Ontological claim / ontological question
Any claim or question about whether something exists, or about the basic nature of its existence, is ontological. "Do thoughts exist independently of the brain?" is an ontological question. "Are colors real properties of objects, or just experiences in the mind?" is an ontological question.

5. Ontological security
This one appears in social science and psychology, and it means something slightly different: a person's fundamental sense that their existence and identity are stable and real. Someone with strong ontological security feels confident and grounded in who they are. The word is used here because it refers not to achievements or relationships, but to the bedrock sense of being — of simply existing as a coherent self.
Ontological vs. Words It's Often Confused With

These three adjectives often appear together in philosophy, and mixing them up is easy:

Ontological — relating to existence and being. ("Does this thing exist? What is it, at the most fundamental level?")

Epistemological — relating to knowledge. ("How do we know things? What counts as knowledge? How certain can we be?")

Metaphysical — relating to the nature of reality beyond the physical. This is the broadest of the three. Ontology is actually a branch of metaphysics, so every ontological question is also metaphysical, but not every metaphysical question is ontological. Questions about time, causation, and free will are metaphysical but not purely ontological.

A simple memory anchor: Onto = being/existence. Think of it as "what's on the table of reality — what's actually there?"
The Feeling of an Ontological Question

One of the clearest ways to recognize an ontological question is by how it makes you feel: slightly dizzy, like the ground is shifting. That's because ontological questions attack the foundations, not the surface.

"Is this table made of oak?" is not ontological.
"Is this table even a single, unified thing, or just a collection of atoms that we agreed to call one thing?" — that is ontological.

"Does Santa Claus exist?" asked by a child is not really ontological.
"Does a fictional character like Hamlet exist in any meaningful sense, and if so, in what mode of existence?" — that is ontological.

"Is God powerful?" is theological.
"Does God exist?" — that is ontological.

Ontological means: relating to the fundamental nature of existence — to what things are and whether they are real at the deepest possible level.

Use it when you're talking about:

  • Whether something exists, and in what sense
  • What kind of thing something fundamentally is
  • The most basic categories of reality
  • Arguments or questions that operate at the level of being itself, not evidence or observation

It is one of the deepest words in the philosophical vocabulary — and once you have it, you'll start noticing that some of the most important arguments in philosophy, science, religion, and even everyday life are secretly ontological arguments in disguise.
